decisions.quote: The current study sought to replicate the GEL model and explore if session frequency moderates the influence that the number of sessions has on the rate of change in psychotherapy. An archived naturalistic data set with a US university counseling center sample (n=1,207), with treatment progress measured using the Outcome Questionnaire-45 (Lambert et al., 1996), was used.

corrected_value.authors: Dean, D. L., Lowry, P. B., & Humpherys, S.
corrected_value.title: Profiling the research productivity of tenured Information Systems faculty at U.S. institutions.

decisions.quote: Dean, Lowry and Humpherys (2011) examined this question by collecting the pre-promotion publication records of IS faculty members, and found that they “publish in high numbers” in CS and engineering journals (23% of their “top tier” articles) and in non-IS business journals (22%; Dean, Lowry, & Humpherys, 2011, pp. 9, 12). Following their procedures, we limited our sample to recent cases of designated IS scholars in U.S. business schools, but used a more recent time frame, and found very similar results. Details of our modest replication of their study are found in the Appendix (Table A1).
decisions.reason: In addition to replicating the focal journal-quality ranking study of Lowry et al. (2013) (shipped row 2301, 10.25300/misq/2013/37.4.01, blind target 0), Stewart and Cotton (2018) conduct and report an independent empirical replication of Dean, Lowry, and Humpherys (2011) ('Profiling the research productivity of tenured Information Systems faculty at U.S. institutions', MIS Quarterly 35: 1-15) in Section 2.2 and Appendix A1 (Table A1), collecting pre-promotion publication records for a new 2006-2015 sample of 67 promoted IS faculty and comparing publication shares across CS/engineering and non-IS business journals against Dean et al.'s 1990-2008 sample of 210 scholars. Dean et al. (2011) is a distinct empirical study absent from the shipped rows.

decisions.quote: Prior evidence suggests that listeners leniently interpret sentences with errors when they are produced by a second-language speaker. Here, we aim to replicate this lenient listener effect for second-language speakers, and to determine whether this effect extends to speakers with a language disorder.
decisions.reason: The primary source text for d2f57b9fdad23ed5 contains only the title, author list, and abstract. Although the abstract states that the study replicates the lenient listener effect for second-language speakers, it includes no citations or bibliographic details identifying the original work being replicated. Consequently, the primary source text cannot verify the identity of the target study or determine whether it is already represented by shipped row 1251 (Gibson et al. 2017, 10.1177/0956797617690277).
